title: Mating activates neuroendocrine pathways signaling hunger in Drosophila females
abstract: Mated females reallocate resources to offspring production, causing changes to nutritional requirements and challenges to energy homeostasis. Although observed across species, the neural and endocrine mechanisms that regulate the nutritional needs of mated females are not well understood. Here, we find that mated Drosophila melanogaster females increase sugar intake, which is regulated by the activity of sexually dimorphic insulin receptor (Lgr3) neurons. In virgins, Lgr3+ cells have reduced activity as they receive inhibitory input from active, female-specific pCd-2 cells, restricting sugar intake. During copulation, males deposit sex peptide into the female reproductive tract, which silences a three-tier mating status circuit and initiates the female postmating response. We show that pCd-2 neurons also become silenced after mating due to the direct synaptic input from the mating status circuit. Thus, in mated females pCd-2 inhibition is attenuated, activating downstream Lgr3+ neurons and promoting sugar intake. Together, this circuit transforms the mated signal into a long-term hunger signal. Our results demonstrate that the mating circuit alters nutrient sensing centers to increase feeding in mated females, providing a mechanism to increase intake in anticipation of the energetic costs associated with reproduction.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This study has seen strong scholarly uptake for a 2023 eLife article, with 29 OpenAlex citations and placement in the top 10% of papers in its field and year. Its influence is especially visible in a fast-moving citation trail dominated by preprints, alongside use as a methodological and conceptual reference in Drosophila neurobiology and reproductive physiology.

Full narrative

Laturney, Sterne, and Scott identify a neuroendocrine route through which mating shifts feeding behavior in Drosophila melanogaster females, helping explain how reproductive state reshapes nutrient demand. The article’s impact is already clear in the scholarly record: it has 29 OpenAlex citations and is in the top 10% of papers in its field and publication year, suggesting that the work was taken up quickly and is resonating within an active research area.

The citation pattern points to rapid diffusion through the literature. Nearly half of the documented reuse comes from preprints, and the most recent citing works continue to appear in adjacent areas such as Drosophila sensory circuitry, sexual dimorphism, and ovulation-related signaling. That pattern suggests the paper is being read not only as a findings paper, but also as a framework for thinking about how reproductive state, endocrine signaling, and feeding circuits are linked.

The downstream landscape is concentrated but broad enough to indicate cross-fertilization across related subfields. Most citing works cluster in neurobiology and insect physiology, with additional attention in animal behavior, developmental biology, and genetics. Several recent citations appear in journals such as eLife, Development, iScience, and BMC Biology, reinforcing the article’s relevance to researchers studying endocrine control, behavior, and physiology in model organisms.

Beyond citations, the record shows substantial scholarly reuse: 30 downstream works are documented, and the article is associated with 16 RRID-linked methods references, supporting its role as a methodological anchor. There is also a small teaching signal, with the paper explicitly referenced in a recorded Open Box Science video, indicating that it has begun to circulate in educational and seminar contexts as well as in research literature.

The broader dissemination record is comparatively modest outside scholarly channels. Event-data mentions and scite-based support/contradiction counts are not available here, so the safest reading is that the article’s influence is best evidenced by citations, reuse, and disciplinary uptake rather than by public-facing attention. The work is openly accessible, and its open infrastructure, peer-review records, and linked data repositories align with the kind of discoverable, reusable scholarship that tends to support continued citation and reuse over time.
